scenes.title: Haven — a storefront written by AI
scenes.caption: This is Haven, a mid-market furniture brand. Every section, every product card, every line of copy was generated by an AI in real time. There's no template underneath this. The engine decided the layout, the hero product, the editorial tone — all from a single visit with zero shopper data. This isn't personalization bolted onto a theme. The storefront itself is the output of an inference call.

scenes.title: The Gatherer default
scenes.caption: A fresh visitor defaults to the Gatherer persona — someone browsing for inspiration. So the layout leads editorial, pulls one hero forward, gives the grid room to breathe. The same catalog renders completely differently for a different persona. The brand config tells the AI what editorial means for a furniture store — warm, tactile, specific about materials. Not generic lifestyle copy.

scenes.title: Observe — making the invisible visible
scenes.caption: This is the telemetry surface. Every signal the system receives shows up in the timeline. The persona vector shows the engine's current belief — gatherer thirty-eight percent, hunter twenty-five. Right now it's working from priors only — device type, page view, category. Every inference decision is traceable. When the layout changes, you can see exactly which signals caused it.

scenes.title: Search triggers a shift
scenes.caption: The shopper searches for 'dorm room desk' — and the entire layout transforms. Dense grid, cheapest first, quick-add buttons, sort and filter controls. Same catalog, same request, completely different experience. The budget-driven shopper gets what they expect without the merchant configuring a separate landing page. The engine re-ran persona inference mid-request and picked a new layout strategy.

scenes.title: Why the layout changed
scenes.caption: Here's what happened. That search query fired two inference rules — hunter-keyword matched 'dorm' and 'desk,' price-sensitivity pushed the budget modifier up. Hunter jumped from twenty-five to forty-one percent, overtook gatherer. The layout followed the belief. The persona engine and the layout engine are separate — one updates beliefs, the other renders from beliefs. No coupling between signal interpretation and visual output.

scenes.title: Refinement chat — steering by conversation
scenes.caption: If the layout doesn't match what the shopper wants, they can say so directly. Each message becomes a constraint that stacks with previous ones. The quick actions are brand-aware — furniture gets price caps and material filters, audio would get battery life and noise cancellation. The shopper co-authors the storefront through natural language instead of clicking through faceted search.

scenes.title: Constraints stack
scenes.caption: One refinement in — 'under eight hundred dollars, small apartment.' The AI responds in Haven's voice, narrows to twelve pieces, explains its reasoning. Every refinement compounds — the next message builds on this one. That's a fundamentally different interaction model than filters. The shopper is having a conversation with the storefront, and the storefront remembers context.

scenes.title: Refinement in Observe
scenes.caption: On the telemetry side, that generation logged as type 'refine' — same model, same pipeline, but no cache because constraints are session-specific. A fresh generation on Haiku ran in about eight seconds, cost six-tenths of a cent. Refinements are the expensive path — but they're also the high-intent path. The shopper who refines is closer to buying.

scenes.title: Same engine, different world
scenes.caption: Same codebase, same inference engine, same AI. But this is Volt — consumer audio. Dark aesthetic, Space Grotesk typography, completely different product vocabulary. The engine adapted entirely from the brand config. There is no Volt-specific application code. Adding a new brand is a config file, not a feature branch.

scenes.title: The AI writes differently here
scenes.caption: Notice the copy. For Haven it writes about fabric and proportions. For Volt it leads with drivers, battery life, codec support — because the persona definitions tell the model that a researcher in consumer audio compares LDAC versus aptX, not thread count. The editorial register flips from warm to precise. Same model, different domain knowledge injected through config.

scenes.title: Ember — third brand, third aesthetic
scenes.caption: Third brand. Ember — outdoor lifestyle, centered on fire and gathering. Libre Baskerville for the rugged editorial feel, terracotta and olive palette. Three brands, three visual identities, three product domains — zero custom UI code per brand. The engine reads the config and generates everything from typography to product descriptions to layout strategy.

scenes.title: The Gatherer layout, Ember voice
scenes.caption: Same gatherer persona, same layout logic — but the copy lands differently because the brand config defines what warm-and-rugged means for outdoor gear. 'Double-wall stainless, smokeless burn, nineteen-inch diameter, fits six chairs around it' — that's specific product knowledge, not marketing fluff. The voice guidance is in the config, not in the model.

scenes.title: The moat is configuration, not code
scenes.caption: This is the actual Ember brand config. Channel ID, category map, theme tokens, persona definitions, voice guidance. A hundred and fifty lines of TypeScript. Write this file, run enrichment on the catalog, deploy — that's the entire checklist for a new brand. The competitive moat isn't the AI. Anyone can call an LLM. The moat is teaching it to write like a specific brand for a specific domain.
